summary: Defines a set of SNMP management objects for monitoring and managing RSVP on a device, written with SMIv2. It builds on the interface attributes of the Integrated Services model. Network managers can use it to inspect reservations.

eli5.summary: It is a dashboard layout that lets a network operator look at, and adjust, the reservations a router is keeping.

questions: how to monitor rsvp with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for inspecting and configuring RSVP state on a router or host.

tldr.problem: Network managers had no standard way to look at, or control, the RSVP sessions, senders, reservations and interfaces on a device.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2206 defines the RSVP-MIB module in SMIv2, with tables for sessions, senders, received and forwarded reservation requests, interface attributes and neighbors, plus two flow notifications.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read RSVP state and, because the path and reservation tables are writable, even create reservations through SNMP instead of RSVP. It works together with the Integrated Services MIB.

facts.label: Tables
facts.value: 6 (session, sender, reservations received, reservations forwarded, interface, neighbor)

today: RFC 2206 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the Integrated Services MIB and is used together with RSVP, which RFC 2205 specifies.

sections.title: What the RSVP MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 2206 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP). It is written with SMIv2, and it manages RSVP within the interface attributes defined in the Integrated Services model, so the Integrated Services MIB is cross-referenced throughout. The compliance statement says that implementing this module requires implementing the Integrated Services MIB as well.

Managed objects live in a virtual information store. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the module itself sits at { mib-2 51 }. Its four branches are rsvpObjects (tables), rsvpGenObjects (global objects), rsvpNotificationsPrefix (traps) and rsvpConformance.
sections.eli5: It is a standard list of questions you can ask a router about its reservations, with a fixed name for each question so every brand answers the same way.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Structured
sections.content:
The MIB has general objects plus six tables: session statistics, session sender, reservation requests received, reservation requests forwarded, RSVP interface attributes and RSVP neighbor.

Because SNMP struggles to describe arbitrarily long or complex messages, the MIB shows the path state and reservation state as though each flow and filter description in an aggregate message had arrived in a separate message. The RFC's example is a RESV message for session 224.1.2.3+UDP+4455 naming senders 1.2.3.4 and 1.2.7.8. It appears as two separate rows, one per sender.

The RFC also introduces textual conventions, RsvpEncapsulation and RefreshInterval. They only make the specification easier to read and do not change the syntax or semantics of any object.
sections.eli5: If one letter lists two senders, the dashboard writes it down as two separate lines, so each line is simple to read.

sections.title: Sessions, Senders and Reservations
sections.content:
The session table (rsvpSessionTable) lists every session seen by the system, with its destination address, IP protocol, port, and counts of senders, receivers and upstream requests. A general object, rsvpBadPackets, counts bad RSVP packets received.

The sender table (rsvpSenderTable) is in essence a list of the valid PATH messages the router or host is receiving. Each row holds the sender's addresses and ports, the previous hop, the sender's TSpec (rate, peak rate, burst, minimum and maximum unit), the refresh interval, and the Adspec details for the guaranteed and controlled-load services.

The reservation tables are the same idea for RESV messages: rsvpResvTable holds requests received, and rsvpResvFwdTable holds requests being sent to upstream neighbors. Rows carry the requested service, TSpec, RSpec and the scope, shared and explicit flags. Per the compliance statement, the forwarded-requests table suits implementations that store upstream reservation messages, but not ones that recompute them at each transmission.
sections.eli5: There is one list for who is talking, one for who wants a reserved lane, and one for the lanes passed along to the next router.

sections.title: Writing State Through SNMP
sections.content:
The path and reservation state tables are writable. This lets a manager perform RSVP reservations without authenticating through RSVP mechanisms, using SNMP mechanisms instead.

State created this way by SNMP does not time out, and it cannot be deleted by receiving an RSVP teardown message. It can only be deleted through SNMP, by writing destroy to the row's RowStatus object, which then initiates a teardown message as if the state had timed out.

To create a new sender or reservation row, the manager first reads the matching NewIndex object (for example rsvpSenderNewIndex, a TestAndIncr object) and writes the value back in the SET that creates the row. If that SET fails with inconsistentValue, the manager repeats the process.

Some address, port and protocol objects may not be changed while the row's RowStatus is active.
sections.eli5: An operator can write a reservation straight onto the router's notepad. Because it came from the operator, it stays until the operator erases it.

sections.title: Interfaces and Neighbors
sections.content:
The interface attributes table (rsvpIfTable), indexed by ifIndex, holds RSVP-specific settings. Information shared with other reservation procedures such as ST-II lives in the Integrated Interface Attributes database instead. Its settings include whether RSVP is enabled, the refresh interval R, the refresh multiple K (default 3), the blockade multiple Kb (default 4), the SEND_TTL value, the route delay (default 200 hundredths of a second, or 2 seconds), and whether UDP encapsulation is forced. It also counts neighbors using UDP only, IP only, or either.

The neighbor table (rsvpNbrTable) lists the neighbors from which RSVP messages are being received, indexed by interface and neighbor address. Each neighbor's encapsulation is ip (IP protocol 46), udp or both. The status object may be used to configure neighbors, and with configured neighbors an implementation may, but need not, limit valid neighbors to those.
sections.eli5: Each network plug has its own settings page, such as how often to repeat messages, and there is a list of the neighbor routers it is hearing from.

sections.title: Notifications and Conformance
sections.content:
Two notifications report flow changes. newFlow says the originating system has installed a new flow in its classifier, or, when reservation authorization is in view, is ready to install one and is requesting authorization. Authorization or refusal can be enacted by writing the Integrated Services variable intSrvFlowStatus. lostFlow says a flow has been removed from the classifier. Both carry the same objects, so a manager can read more detail.

For conformance, the mandatory groups cover sessions, senders, reservations, interfaces and neighbors. The forwarded-reservations group and the notification group are conditional. The notifications are required when the RSVP Policy Module uses an SNMP interface to the Policy Manager. Several sender objects may be implemented read-only rather than read-create, and rsvpSessionRequests is optional.
sections.eli5: The router can ring a bell when a new reserved lane starts or an old one disappears, so the operator does not have to keep checking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is brief. Using an SNMP SET results in an RSVP or Integrated Services reservation under different rules than if the reservation had been negotiated with RSVP. Beyond that, no security considerations exist other than those imposed by SNMP itself.
sections.eli5: Writing a reservation by hand skips RSVP's normal checks, so the usual SNMP protections are what keep it safe.
